title: Gaussian Lévy-Khintchine Exponent: Complex Arithmetic Properties
description: Derives explicit Complex arithmetic properties of the Gaussian Lévy-Khintchine exponent ψ(t) = iμt − σ²t²/2. Proves Re(ψ) = −σ²t²/2 (damping), Im(ψ) = μt (drift), even/odd symmetry of real/imaginary parts, and exp(ψ(0)) = 1. 7 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified using only Mathlib's Complex arithmetic.

mathlibDependencies.description: Re(a-b) = Re(a) - Re(b), Im(a-b) = Im(a) - Im(b): linearity of Re/Im under subtraction
Re(a*b) = Re(a)*Re(b) - Im(a)*Im(b), Im(a*b) = Re(a)*Im(b) + Im(a)*Re(b)

originalContributions: gaussianExponent_re: Re(ψ(t)) = −σ²t²/2 — the Gaussian damping term, proved via Complex.sub_re, Complex.mul_re, Complex.I_re/im, Complex.ofReal_re/im
gaussianExponent_im: Im(ψ(t)) = μt — the drift/oscillation term, proved via Complex.sub_im, Complex.mul_im
gaussianExponent_pure_imaginary: when σ²=0, ψ(t) is purely imaginary (pure rotation, no damping)
gaussianExponent_re_even: Re(ψ(−t)) = Re(ψ(t)) — even symmetry, since (−t)² = t²
gaussianExponent_im_odd: Im(ψ(−t)) = −Im(ψ(t)) — odd symmetry, since μ(−t) = −μt
gaussianCharFn_at_zero: exp(ψ(0)) = 1 — characteristic function equals 1 at origin

overview.historicalContext: The Lévy-Khintchine representation theorem (1934-1937) characterizes all infinitely divisible distributions via their characteristic functions. For a Gaussian N(μ, σ²), the exponent in the characteristic function E[e^{itX}] = exp(ψ(t)) is ψ(t) = iμt − σ²t²/2. The real part −σ²t²/2 causes exponential decay of the characteristic function (the 'damping' or 'diffusion' component) while the imaginary part μt causes oscillation (the 'drift' component). Understanding these components explicitly is fundamental to proving the Central Limit Theorem and characterizing limiting distributions.
overview.problemStatement: The parent entry CentralLimitTheoremOQ01OQ02 defines gaussianExponent and proves ψ(0) = 0 via simp. What are the explicit Complex arithmetic lemmas involved, and what further properties of ψ follow from elementary complex arithmetic without additional probability theory?
overview.text: ψ(t) = ofReal(μt)·I − ofReal(σ²t²/2). The real part: Re(ofReal(μt)·I) = (μt)·Re(I) − 0·Im(I) = (μt)·0 = 0, and Re(ofReal(σ²t²/2)) = σ²t²/2, so Re(ψ) = 0 − σ²t²/2 = −σ²t²/2. The imaginary part: Im(ofReal(μt)·I) = (μt)·Im(I) + 0·Re(I) = μt, and Im(ofReal(σ²t²/2)) = 0, so Im(ψ) = μt − 0 = μt. Symmetry: Re(ψ(−t)) = −σ²(−t)²/2 = −σ²t²/2 = Re(ψ(t)) (even); Im(ψ(−t)) = μ(−t) = −μt = −Im(ψ(t)) (odd).
overview.proofStrategy: Unfold gaussianExponent via simp only and apply the standard Complex arithmetic lemmas: Complex.sub_re/im for subtraction, Complex.mul_re/im for multiplication, Complex.ofReal_re/im for coercions, Complex.I_re/im for the imaginary unit. Use ring to close arithmetic goals. For symmetry, apply the proved gaussianExponent_re/im lemmas and ring.
keyInsights: The key Complex arithmetic decomposition: (a·I − b).re = 0 − b.re = −b.re and (a·I − b).im = a·1 − b.im = a (for real a, b)
Even real part implies |φ(t)| = |φ(−t)|: the modulus of the Gaussian characteristic function is symmetric
Odd imaginary part corresponds to conjugate symmetry: φ(−t) = conj(φ(t)) for real-valued distributions
exp(ψ(0)) = 1 is the normalization condition: all characteristic functions equal 1 at the origin

The proof pattern — simp only [Complex.sub_re, Complex.mul_re, Complex.I_re, Complex.I_im, Complex.ofReal_re, Complex.ofReal_im] then ring — is the idiomatic Lean 4 approach to computing Re/Im of Complex expressions, and generalizes to any polynomial combination of ofReal values and I.
prerequisites: Complex number arithmetic (Complex.sub_re, Complex.mul_re, Complex.ofReal_re, Complex.I_re)

sections.title: Module Header and Imports
sections.summary: Imports Complex.Circle, Log.Basic, Complex.Basic, and Tactic from Mathlib. Imports CentralLimitTheoremOQ01OQ02 for the gaussianExponent definition. Opens Complex and CentralLimitTheoremOQ01OQ02 namespaces. Module docstring documents all 7 theorems and the proof strategy.
sections.mathContext: The Gaussian Lévy-Khintchine exponent is defined as $\psi(\mu, \sigma^2, t) = \text{ofReal}(\mu t) \cdot I - \text{ofReal}(\sigma^2 t^2/2) \in \mathbb{C}$, so that $\varphi(t) = e^{\psi(t)}$ is the characteristic function of $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

sections.title: Real and Imaginary Parts of ψ
sections.summary: Re(ψ(t)) = −σ²t²/2 and Im(ψ(t)) = μt proved via Complex arithmetic lemmas
sections.content: gaussianExponent_re uses Complex.sub_re + Complex.mul_re + I_re/im + ofReal_re/im then ring. gaussianExponent_im uses Complex.sub_im + Complex.mul_im + I_re/im + ofReal_re/im then ring.

sections.title: Pure Imaginary Case (σ² = 0)
sections.summary: When σ² = 0, ψ(t) = iμt is purely imaginary — pure rotation with no damping
sections.content: gaussianExponent_pure_imaginary proves ψ μ 0 t = (μ*t)*I directly by simp. gaussianExponent_zero_sigma_re derives Re = 0 from gaussianExponent_re.

sections.title: Even/Odd Symmetry of ψ
sections.content: gaussianExponent_re_even: simp [gaussianExponent_re] then ring, using (−t)² = t². gaussianExponent_im_odd: simp [gaussianExponent_im] then ring, using μ(−t) = −μt.

sections.title: Characteristic Function at t = 0
sections.summary: exp(ψ(0)) = 1 — every characteristic function is normalized to 1 at the origin
sections.content: gaussianCharFn_at_zero: rw [gaussianExponent_zero] reduces to exp(0) = 1, then Complex.exp_zero.

conclusion.summary: 7 properties of the Gaussian Lévy-Khintchine exponent proved via elementary Complex arithmetic. No probability theory needed beyond the definition — all results follow from the algebraic structure of Complex numbers.
conclusion.implications: These results provide the foundation for proving the CLT via characteristic functions: the even/odd symmetry corresponds to conjugate symmetry of the characteristic function φ(t) = exp(ψ(t)), which is a hallmark of real-valued random variables.
openQuestions: Prove that exp(ψ(t)) is the characteristic function of N(μ, σ²): ∫ e^{itx} (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)) dx = exp(iμt − σ²t²/2)
Show that exp(ψ_n(t)) → exp(ψ(t)) pointwise implies X_n →^d N(μ, σ²) — the Lévy continuity theorem applied to the CLT
Prove that |exp(ψ(t))| = exp(Re(ψ(t))) = exp(−σ²t²/2), showing the Gaussian characteristic function decays as a Gaussian in t — connecting Re(ψ) to the modulus decay rate
